extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in media criticism, journalists and editors
extracted.subtask_description: A news/opinion article examining a high-profile instance of alleged self-plagiarism by a magazine writer, discussing journalistic standards, editorial responses, and the boundaries of acceptable reuse. Useful for understanding norms and practices in journalism ethics and online editorial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / no self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Material published should be original; copying from one’s own previously published work (self-plagiarism) is treated as an offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that Lehrer published pieces whose first three paragraphs were nearly identical across two outlets. The piece states that self-plagiarism is "an offense bound to be discovered," and quotes NewYorker.com editor Nicholas Thompson: "I think everybody knows that... they can't do this." The article treats the reuse of previously published text as unacceptable when represented as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution and accurate sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must attribute sources correctly and not imply direct conversations or firsthand knowledge when the information originated elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a note appended to Lehrer's January 2012 article informed readers that Lehrer had implied a comment by Noam Chomsky had been told to him directly, when in fact the comment originated in another journalist’s Technology Review article. The piece frames this as a failure of attribution/accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about reuse of material (lectures and prior publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing material from paid lectures or previously published works without disclosure is problematic and can be unacceptable in blog posts and newspaper articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Lehrer recycles material for his paid lectures and that "representing that material as original in blog posts and newspaper articles is another matter, one that few editors—or competing writers—are likely to countenance." Implicit guidance: disclose reuse or avoid representing reused material as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial correction and disclosure practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When duplication or attribution errors are discovered, editors should append notes, acknowledge the duplication, and apologize or correct the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NewYorker.com appended notes to all five of Lehrer's posts noting where information had been pilfered and adding, apologetically, "We regret the duplication of the material." The piece presents such appended notes as the publication’s remedial response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using editorial platforms to promote work without originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should not use high-profile outlets to promote books or build reputation by reusing non-original material; doing so breaches ethical expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues Lehrer used his high-profile platforms at Wired and The New Yorker to "push his books and burnish his reputation without doing sufficiently original work," framing that behavior as ethically suspect and a reason for professional criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting duplication via targeted text search
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplications can be discovered by searching for distinctive quotations, anecdotes, or proper names in search engines like Google.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes a method: take passages (famous quotations, distinctive anecdotes, proper names) and paste them into Google—useful results rise to the top and quickly reveal repeated material. The article treats this as an effective way the community uncovers self-plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial expectations for online content (NewYorker stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online editorial operations expect original, breaking, or distinctive content; duplication of material on the site is explicitly unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context on NewYorker's digital expansion and Nicholas Thompson's statements: the site has grown its online presence and traffic, and Thompson characterized the duplication as serious—"He understands the rules. It’s definitely not going to happen again." The article implies staff are expected to adhere to policies against duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate about permissible repurposing of long-form into blog posts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an unresolved question whether repurposing material from long-form print articles into blog posts constitutes plagiarism and under what conditions it is allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece raises the question explicitly: "Is it plagiarism when you’re copying from yourself? Can’t a journalist repurpose material from a long-form print article into a blog post?" It does not offer a definitive rule but presents the debate and shows the publication’s practical response (corrections) as part of how such cases are treated.
